Reviewer #3:

The study describes three experiments that investigated the influence of increased feedback time delay in the ability of human subjects to maintain stable upright balance and their ability to learn/adapt to control balance at time delays values that are greater than those predicted to be possible based on existing simple feedback control models of balance. The studies made use of a unique robot balance device that allowed the generation of continuous body motion as a function of a time-delayed version of the corrective ankle torque generated by the subject as they swayed.

The experiments quantified changes in body sway behaviors as a function of added time delay and characterized the time course of improvements in balance control as subjects learned to stand with a long delay value imposed by the robotic device. The learning was acquired over multiple training sessions and was demonstrated both by a reduction over time in sway measures and by changes in psychophysical measures that demonstrated a reduction in a subject's indication of the occurrence of unexpected body motions. Additionally, the learned ability to control balance with an added time delay was very well retained at 3 months post training.

A final experiment used electrical vestibular stimulation (EVS) to demonstrate the changing contribution of vestibular information to balance control following a transient increase in time delay. This experiment demonstrated a marked reduction in activity in the soleus muscle that was correlated with the EVS following the onset of an added feedback time delay indicating that the added delay caused a reduction in the vestibular contribution to balance.

In general, the experiments were appropriately designed and analyzed. Although the number of participants in each experiment were not large, they were sufficient given the rather robust effects observed when time delays were added to be feedback.

The robotic balance device not only permitted manipulation of the time delay, but also guarded against subjects actually falling when they swayed beyond the normal range of sways compatible with stable balance. This artificial stabilization of balance beyond the normal range permitted subjects to recover from what would otherwise have been a fall and to immediately continue their attempts to learn a balance strategy that was able to overcome the detrimental effects of increased feedback delay. Thus the training procedure was likely much more effective than if trials had been stopped when sway moved beyond the normal range. One imagines such a training device could have important uses in rehabilitation of balance deficits.

But this artificial stabilization also interfered with one of the balance measures used to quantify the influence of added time delay. Specifically, the RMS sway measure used by the authors did not distinguish between time periods when the subject was being artificially stabilized and the time periods when sway was within the normal sway range. Thus the results that were based on the RMS sway measure were not convincing. But fortunately a sway velocity variance measure was also used to quantify sway behavior as a function of time delay and this measure only used data that was within the normal range of sway.

Overall results are an important addition to knowledge related to how humans control standing balance and demonstrate an ability to learn, with training, to balance with unexpectedly long delays between control action and the resulting body motion.

Overall results are clearly presented but this reviewer has some suggestions for improvement.

1. Experiment 1 quantifies changes in balance control as a function of added time delay by measuring RMS sway amplitude and sway velocity variance. It seems incorrect to use the entire 60 seconds of data in the calculation of RMS sway when there are periods of sway beyond the 3 deg backward and 6 deg forward sway balance limits since the backboard motion is artificially stabilized in the region outside the balance limits. It is only with detailed reading of the methods that the reader understands that the backboard motion is artificially stabilized at extremes of sway so this makes a complete understanding of the RMS sway results presented in Figure 2 difficult. But the problem is not fixed by just making the artificial stabilization methods more evident when presenting the Figure 2 results. The problem is that this RMS sway calculation is not representative of the overall subject-controlled sway behavior when there are periods in the trails when the sway was not controlled by the subject (which occurred frequently with longer delays). This reviewer suggests that a much more useful measure would be to calculate and display the percentage of time that subjects were maintaining control within the balance limits. It would be similarly informative to see this type of percentage measure used to track the Experiment 2 learning results in addition to the velocity variance measures shown in Figure 3.

2. In Experiment 3, group data results show changes in muscle activation evoked by electrical vestibular stimulation based on the 489 of 588 trials on which subjects signaled that they detected an unexpected balance motion. But what about the other 99 trials when subjects did not signal unexpected balance motion? Since the authors suggest there is a possible linkage between the time course of vestibular decline and the detection of unexpected motion, it may be that there was a slower (longer time constant) or reduced amplitude of vestibular decline on the 99 trials where unexpected motion was not detected. Such a finding would strengthen the notion of a linkage between vestibular inhibition and motion detection. Alternatively, if the vestibular declines were indistinguishable between trials with and without unexpected motion this would suggest that the linkage was not tight and something else may be involved. In either case this comparison would be useful. Additionally, it seems that 99 trials should be enough data since Figure 6 shows good results from a single subject based on 77 trials.

3. The section on pages 23 and 24 discusses alternative models that might be able to explain how subjects can learn to tolerate long time delays. I believe that all of the references to alternative models are to models that would be classified as continuous control models as opposed to intermittent control schemes that have been proposed as an alternative (e.g. Ian Loram references such as Loram et al., J Physiol 589.2:307-324, 2011, Gawthrop, Loram, Lakie, Biol Cybern 101:131-146, 2009, and the Morasso reference in the authors manuscript). It seems that Loram's work has shown that it is possible to visually control an unstable load with properties similar to those of a human body using an intermittent control scheme. This intermittent control scheme should be referenced. But beyond just mentioning these alternative control structures as possibilities, do the authors know of actual simulations of these models that can demonstrate that an inverted pendulum system can be made stable with the extremely long time delays that the authors investigated?

4. Several places in the manuscript the authors refer to estimates of maximal time delays based on simpler feedback control models. Specifically, the Bingham et al. 2011 and the van der Kooij and Peterka, 2011 references are given. But the values of the maximal time delays are not consistent across the various mentions of these two references. Here is a listing of those mentions:

- Line 78: ~300 ms

- Line 406: 340-430 ms

- Line 667: ~400 ms

- Line 678: ~400 ms

This reviewer could find mention of 340 ms in the van der Kooij and Peterka paper, but it seems that the Bingham paper did not really investigate time delay in detail and that paper also was investigating body motion in the frontal plane that has considerably different lower body dynamics compared to a single segment inverted pendulum.

5. The authors indicated that analysis programs and data will be made publicly available upon acceptance for publication.

results.result: Experiment 1 demonstrated that imposed sensorimotor delays progressively destabilized standing balance. Sway velocity variance increased with delay magnitude (reaching maximum at 400 ms: 21.08 ± 15.41 [°/s]²), and all participants exceeded virtual balance limits when delays were ≥200 ms.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C36 and C95 provide converging evidence from Experiment 1 with appropriate statistical analysis (main effect of delay, p<0.001) and clear quantitative measurements. The data show systematic increases in sway variability and decreases in time within balance limits as delays increased, with critical threshold around 200 ms.

results.result: Participants learned to balance with a 400 ms imposed delay through training over 5 days (100 min total). Sway velocity variance decreased by ~80% and time within balance limits increased by 51%, with time constants of ~28-33 min. Learning was partially retained after 3 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C52 provide detailed quantitative evidence of learning with exponential fits, statistical comparisons, and retention data. The results demonstrate that humans can learn to control balance with total delays of 500-560 ms (400 ms imposed + 100-160 ms physiological), exceeding the predicted critical delay of 300-340 ms from computational models.

results.result: Vestibular-evoked muscle responses (measured via EVS-EMG coherence, gain, and cross-covariance) were attenuated by imposed delays before training, with responses decreasing for delays ≥200 ms. After training, vestibular responses partially recovered, with significant increases in cross-covariance amplitudes for delays ≥200 ms (p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C69 provide comprehensive vestibular testing data with appropriate frequency-domain and time-domain analyses. Statistical tests show significant delay × learning interactions (p<0.001), and planned comparisons demonstrate recovery of vestibular responses after training. The partial recovery supports the interpretation that the nervous system updated its sensorimotor estimates.

results.result: Perceptual testing showed that imposed delays triggered perceptions of unexpected standing motion, with detection probability increasing from 4% at 50 ms to 100% at 350 ms. After training, psychometric functions shifted rightward, with detection thresholds increasing from 147 ± 21 ms to 192 ± 40 ms post-learning (p=0.032).
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C81 provide perceptual data with appropriate psychometric analysis using Bayesian curve fitting. The rightward shift in thresholds after training indicates that larger delays were needed to evoke perceptions of unexpected motion, supporting the interpretation that participants learned to associate delayed feedback with self-generated commands.

results.result: Experiment 3 tracked the time course of responses to transient 200 ms delays. Vestibular coherence attenuated with a time constant of 1.5 ± 0.6 s (63.2% attenuation), and perceptual detection occurred at 3.4 ± 1.8 s on average, corresponding to ~90% reduction in coherence and 73% reduction in gain.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C94 provide detailed temporal analysis linking vestibular attenuation, sway variability, and perceptual detection. The time-frequency analysis appropriately characterizes the dynamics of vestibular response changes, and the temporal alignment between vestibular attenuation and perceptual detection supports the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: Learning generalized across delays despite training only at 400 ms. Vestibular responses and sway behavior improved at multiple untrained delays (20-500 ms), suggesting the nervous system broadly updated its control rather than specifically recalibrating to the 400 ms delay.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 and C128-C129 correctly identify that training was only at 400 ms, yet improvements occurred at other delays. This generalization is well-documented in the vestibular and perceptual testing data (C63-C64, C68-C69, C80-C81), supporting the inference of broad sensorimotor recalibration.

results.result: The main mechanistic conclusion is that the nervous system learns to accommodate balance sensorimotor delays by causally linking delayed whole-body sensory feedback (initially interpreted as imposed motion) to self-generated balance motor commands, involving sensorimotor recalibration rather than simple sensory reweighting.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C10, C25, C103, C148 state the main mechanistic interpretation, which is supported by the convergence of vestibular recovery (C60-C64), perceptual threshold shifts (C76-C78), and behavioral improvements (C41-C42). The inference that this involves recalibration (C113-C115) is justified by the partial return of vestibular responses and generalization across delays, which cannot be explained by simple gain reduction.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that errors increase with feedback delays, the brain can learn to expect delays up to 430 ms in upper-limb tasks, standing balance has inherent delays of ~100-160 ms, and computational models predict balance cannot be stabilized with delays >300-340 ms.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C15 are appropriately cited background claims that establish the context for the study. The citations appear relevant and the claims are consistent with established knowledge in motor control and balance research.

results.result: Prior work demonstrates that novel sensorimotor relationships initially disrupt performance but can be learned through recalibration, including vestibular feedback manipulations, delayed touch perception, and cerebellar mechanisms for updating sensorimotor predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C19, C116-C120, C124-C126 provide appropriate citations to relevant prior work on sensorimotor adaptation, vestibular recalibration, temporal recalibration, and neural mechanisms. These establish the theoretical framework for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: Discussion of control models: optimal controllers can theoretically stabilize standing with large delays but decline with accelerations; intermittent control may be a solution when delays rule out continuous control; sensory reweighting predicts gain decreases with delays.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C112 appropriately cite relevant computational modeling literature and discuss alternative control strategies. The authors acknowledge (C110) that their study did not explicitly test these different controllers, which is an appropriate limitation statement.

results.result: The authors discuss interpretational challenges: while vestibular and perceptual changes may reflect balance errors, it is unclear what specific component of standing behavior is attributable to prediction errors versus other factors like control policy changes or movement kinematics.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C137 appropriately acknowledge limitations in causal interpretation. The authors correctly note (C133) that they cannot definitively separate prediction error effects from other factors, and suggest (C134-C135) alternative explanations with appropriate citations. This represents appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: Clinical implications: The standing balance system can be trained to accommodate larger delays than predicted, which may benefit clinical populations with increased neural delays due to aging or disease. Training with delays might enable targeted rehabilitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C139 are supported by the experimental findings showing learning beyond predicted limits. However, C141 is speculative about clinical applications without supporting data from clinical populations. The translation from healthy young adults to clinical populations requires validation.

results.result: Limitation: The experimental manipulation delayed whole-body motion relative to ankle torques, but did not delay all somatosensory signals (muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, cutaneous receptors), which may have created sensory conflicts affecting learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C144 appropriately identify a methodological limitation. The authors correctly note that their manipulation selectively delayed some sensory feedback but not others, which could have influenced the results. This is an important caveat for interpretation.

results.result: Methods: 46 healthy adults participated across three experiments using a robotic balance simulator with imposed delays. Vestibular responses were measured using EVS-EMG coherence, gain, and cross-covariance. Perceptual testing used button presses to detect unexpected motion.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C168 describe the methods with appropriate detail. The robotic system, vestibular stimulation, and analysis techniques are well-established methods cited appropriately (C153-C154, C167-C168). Sample sizes are clearly stated for each experiment.

results.result: General principle: Human standing balance relies on self-motion estimates that accommodate for inherent sensory and motor delays, enabling detection of unexpected movements and corrective responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 state general principles about balance control that are well-established in the field and form the conceptual foundation for the study. These are appropriately characterized as knowledge claims.

results.result: After training, vestibular contributions partially returned to baseline levels, with every participant showing significant biphasic muscle responses at all delays post-training, and cross-covariance amplitudes significantly larger for delays ≥200 ms.
results.evaluation: This result is already covered in the vestibular testing result above but emphasizes the completeness of recovery (C61 - every participant showed responses). The statistical evidence (C63-C64) strongly supports partial recovery.
